extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, EPO examiners, IP policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether method claims (diagnostic, therapeutic, imaging) are excluded from patentability under EPC Article 52(4)/53(c) in light of the Enlarged Board of Appeal (G-1/07) decision. Focuses on when a physical/interventional step makes a method unpatentable and how claims may avoid exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a surgical/therapeutic/diagnostic step excludes the method
rubrics_metrics.description: A method claim falls under the prohibition of patenting methods for treatment by therapy or surgery (now Article 53(c) EPC) if it 'comprises or encompasses at least one feature defining a physical activity or action that constitutes a method step for treatment of a human or animal body by surgery or therapy' or is a diagnostic method practised on the human or animal body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of one such step in a multi-step method is sufficient to exclude the entire claimed method from patentability; this applies even if other steps are non-surgical or non-therapeutic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of 'treatment by surgery' is not limited to therapeutic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of the term 'treatment by surgery' is not to be interpreted as being confined to surgical methods pursuing a therapeutic purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surgical methods that are non-therapeutic or not directed to restoring health can nonetheless fall within the exclusion; the historical/legal context and ratio legis do not justify limiting the term to curative surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional medical skill and substantial health risk are indicators of 'surgery'
rubrics_metrics.description: An invasive step that 'represents a substantial physical intervention on the body which requires professional medical expertise to be carried out and which entails a substantial health risk even when carried out with the required professional care and expertise' is covered by the exclusion of treatment by surgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: an injection into the heart; assess whether the step requires professional skills and carries substantial health risk even when performed properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine/minor invasive techniques without substantial health risk may fall outside the exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding from patentability safe routine techniques, even when of invasive nature, appears to go beyond the purpose of the exclusion; uncritical surgical methods involving only a minor intervention and no substantial health risks need not be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between minor routine interventions (which may be patentable) and invasive interventions requiring specialist skill and entailing substantial risk (which are excluded). Consider both invasiveness and the associated health risk and skill required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic methods practised on the human or animal body are excluded (Article 52(4)/53(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 52(4) EPC (now Article 53(c)) excludes from patentability methods for treatment by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practised on the human or animal body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Enlarged Board previously clarified the exclusion of diagnostic methods in G-1/04; applicants and examiners should treat diagnostic methods practised on the body as potentially excluded subject-matter unless claims are specifically drafted to avoid that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-in-surgical-context does not automatically make a method a surgical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed imaging method is not to be considered as being a 'treatment of the human or animal body by surgery' merely because during a surgical intervention the data obtained by the method immediately allow a surgeon to decide on the course of action to be taken during a surgical intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that the teaching can be used advantageously during surgery does not preclude claiming the method per se; Article 53(c) prohibits patenting surgical methods, not methods that can be used in the context of surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation principles for exclusion clauses (ordinary meaning, object and purpose, give effect to terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of exclusion clauses must follow the rules in the Vienna Convention: look at the ordinary meaning of the terms, the object and purpose ('ratio legis') of the provision, and interpret in a manner that gives effect to all terms of the treaty provision. The Vienna Convention does not mandate a narrower interpretation simply because a provision is an exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ratio legis for excluding methods of treatment is socio-ethical — to free the medical profession from constraints imposed by patents — and must be balanced with ordinary meaning and treaty text when deciding scope of exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims can be construed/drafted to avoid excluded subject-matter if essential features are explicitly specified
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible for a patent claim to be construed in a manner that avoids subject-matter excluded from patent protection provided that the claims 'explicitly specify all of the essential features needed to define the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may present/amend claims to omit or avoid the surgical/therapeutic/diagnostic step, but disclosure rules (requirement to disclose all essential features) will limit how far applicants can strip out excluded steps without losing support/validity. See EBoA confirmation of this principle (G-1/04).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining life and health as a contextual indicator for exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed method 'in which, when carried out, maintaining the life and health of the subject is important and which comprises or encompasses an invasive step representing a substantial physical intervention on the body … is excluded from patentability as a method for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing exclusion, consider whether the method as claimed is performed in contexts where maintaining life/health is important and whether the invasive step is integral to that context; both the purpose of the method in practice and the nature of the step matter.
